topic.title: Linked List
topic.summary: Pointer manipulation under pressure: reversal, fast/slow pointers, dummy nodes, merging — plus the classic LRU cache design and the array vs linked list trade-off.
topic.overview:
**Why interviewers love linked lists.** The problems are short enough to code in 15 minutes, yet they show whether you can re-wire pointers without losing nodes, handle `null` edges, and reach O(1) extra space. They are asked at product companies, service companies and bank/fintech interviews alike.

**What you must be able to do without thinking**
- **Reverse** a list iteratively (and recursively) — it is a building block for reorder list, palindrome check and reverse-in-k-groups.
- Use a **dummy (sentinel) node** so that changing or deleting the head needs no special case.
- Use **fast & slow pointers** to find the middle, detect a cycle (Floyd) or keep a fixed gap (n-th from the end).
- **Merge** two sorted lists — the heart of merge sort.
- Explain **arrays vs linked lists** and design an **LRU cache** (hash map + doubly linked list).

**How to practise**
1. Draw boxes and arrows before coding; mark which arrows change in each step.
2. Before writing `a.next = b`, ask: "do I still hold a reference to the old `a.next`?"
3. Always test: empty list, one node, two nodes, odd vs even length, removing the head.
4. Say the complexity including recursion stack space.

**Node definition used in all solutions**
- JavaScript: `class ListNode { constructor(val = 0, next = null) { this.val = val; this.next = next; } }`
- Python: `class ListNode: def __init__(self, val=0, next=None)`
- Java: `class ListNode { int val; ListNode next; ListNode(int val) {…} ListNode(int val, ListNode next) {…} }`

questions.title: Reverse a Linked List
questions.prompt:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list. Reverse the direction of every link **in place** and return the head of the reversed list.

For example `1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5` becomes `5 → 4 → 3 → 2 → 1`. An empty list stays empty.
constraints: Do it in O(1) extra space (iterative); the recursive version is a common follow-up
hints: You cannot move backwards in a singly linked list — so change the arrows instead of the values.
Walk the list once. At each node, which pointer has to change, and what would you lose if you changed it immediately?
Keep three references: `prev`, `curr` and `next`. Save `next = curr.next`, point `curr.next` at `prev`, then shift `prev` and `curr` one step forward.

approaches.name: Copy values to an array
approaches.idea: Read all values into an array, then write them back in reverse order (or build a new list). Easy but uses O(n) extra memory and changes values instead of links.

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: Reverse the rest of the list recursively, then set `head.next.next = head` and `head.next = null`. Elegant, but each node adds a stack frame.

approaches.name: Iterative three pointers
approaches.idea: Walk once with `prev`, `curr`, `next`, flipping one arrow per step.

solution.summary: Walk the list once with three pointers — `prev`, `curr` and `next`. For each node, save `curr.next`, point `curr.next` back at `prev`, then move both pointers forward; when `curr` becomes null, `prev` is the new head. O(n) time, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** A singly linked list only knows "who is next". Reversing it means every arrow `a → b` must become `b → a`. We can flip one arrow per step as long as we never lose our grip on the rest of the list.

**Steps**
1. `prev = null` (the reversed part is empty), `curr = head`.
2. While `curr` is not null:
   - `next = curr.next` — save the rest of the list **before** touching the arrow.
   - `curr.next = prev` — flip the arrow.
   - `prev = curr`, `curr = next` — move forward.
3. Return `prev`; it points at the old tail, which is the new head.

**Why it is correct.** Invariant: at the start of each iteration, `prev` is the head of the already-reversed prefix and `curr` is the head of the untouched suffix. Each iteration moves exactly one node from the suffix to the front of the prefix, so after n iterations the whole list is reversed.

**Edge cases.** Empty list → the loop never runs and we return `null`. One node → its `next` becomes `null` and it is returned unchanged.

**Recursive version (common follow-up)**
```js
function reverseListRecursive(head) {
  if (head === null || head.next === null) return head; // base case
  const newHead = reverseListRecursive(head.next); // reverse the rest
  head.next.next = head; // the node after me now points back to me
  head.next = null;      // I become the tail
  return newHead;
}
```
It is O(n) time but O(n) stack space, and a list with ~10⁵ nodes can overflow the call stack in Java or Python.

code.code:
def reverse_list(head):
    prev, curr = None, head
    while curr:
        nxt = curr.next   # save the rest of the list
        curr.next = prev  # flip the arrow
        prev = curr
        curr = nxt
    return prev  # prev is the new head

complexity.time: O(n) — every node is visited once
complexity.space: O(1) — only three pointers, no matter how long the list is

keyPoints: Save `curr.next` before overwriting it — that is the whole trick
Return `prev`, not `head` (head is now the tail)
Iterative is O(1) space; recursive is O(n) stack space
Handles empty and single-node lists without special cases
Reversal is a building block for reorder list, palindrome check and reverse-in-k-groups

followUps.question: Can you do it recursively? What does it cost?
followUps.answer: Yes: reverse `head.next` recursively, then `head.next.next = head; head.next = null`. Same O(n) time but O(n) call-stack space, so very long lists can overflow the stack.

followUps.question: Reverse only the nodes between positions left and right.
followUps.answer: Walk a pointer to the node before `left` (use a dummy node in case left = 1), reverse the next `right − left + 1` nodes with the same three-pointer loop, then reconnect the two ends. One pass, O(1) space.

followUps.question: Reverse the list in groups of k.
followUps.answer: Check that k nodes remain, reverse that block with the same loop, connect the previous group tail to the new block head, and continue; leave a final group of fewer than k nodes as is.

questions.title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
questions.prompt: You are given the heads of two linked lists `l1` and `l2`, each already sorted in non-decreasing order. Splice their nodes together into **one sorted list** and return its head. Reuse the existing nodes rather than creating new ones.

examples.explanation: If one list is empty, the answer is simply the other list.

constraints: Both lists are sorted in non-decreasing order
hints: The smallest node overall must be the head of one of the two lists.
Repeatedly compare the two current heads and take the smaller one. How do you avoid special-casing the very first node you take?
Create a dummy node and a `tail` pointer. Append the smaller of `l1`/`l2` to `tail`, advance; when one list runs out, attach the other in one step and return `dummy.next`.

approaches.name: Collect + sort
approaches.idea: Copy all values into an array, sort it, and build a new list. Ignores that the inputs are already sorted.

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: The smaller head wins; set its `next` to the merge of the rest. Short, but uses one stack frame per node.

approaches.name: Iterative with dummy node
approaches.idea: Walk both lists with two pointers, splicing the smaller node onto `tail`.

solution.summary: Use a dummy node and a `tail` pointer: while both lists have nodes, link the smaller head to `tail` and advance that list; then attach the leftover list and return `dummy.next`. O(n + m) time, O(1) extra space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** This is the merge step of merge sort, done with pointers. At every moment the next node of the answer is the smaller of the two current heads.

**Steps**
1. Create `dummy` and set `tail = dummy`. The dummy removes the "is the result still empty?" special case.
2. While both `l1` and `l2` are non-null: link the node with the smaller value to `tail.next`, advance that list, then advance `tail`.
3. One list is now empty. The other is already sorted, so attach it with one assignment: `tail.next = l1 ?? l2`.
4. Return `dummy.next`.

**Why `<=`?** On ties we take from `l1` first, so equal values keep their original relative order — the merge is **stable**, exactly what merge sort needs.

**Edge cases.** Either list empty (the loop never runs and we attach the other one), both empty (returns `null`), lists of very different lengths (the leftover attach is O(1)).

complexity.time: O(n + m) — every node is linked exactly once
complexity.space: O(1) — nodes are re-linked, only a dummy and a few pointers are allocated

keyPoints: Dummy node avoids special-casing the head
Compare current heads, splice the smaller one, advance
Attach the remaining list in one step — no loop needed
`<=` keeps the merge stable
This is the merge step of merge sort; it generalises to merging k lists with a min-heap

followUps.question: How would you merge k sorted lists?
followUps.answer: Push the head of each list into a min-heap keyed by value; repeatedly pop the smallest, append it, and push its `next`. O(N log k) for N total nodes. Alternatively merge lists in pairs (divide and conquer), also O(N log k).

followUps.question: Can you write it recursively?
followUps.answer: If either list is empty return the other; otherwise the smaller head’s `next` becomes `merge(smaller.next, other)` and you return the smaller head. O(n + m) stack space.

questions.title: Linked List Cycle (Floyd’s Tortoise and Hare)
questions.prompt:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, return `true` if some node can be reached again by repeatedly following `next` (i.e. the list contains a **cycle**), otherwise `false`.

Do it in O(1) extra memory.

examples.explanation: Following next from 6 goes back to 3 forever.

examples.input: single node whose next points to itself

constraints: Node values may repeat — compare node identity, not values
hints: The simple approach remembers every node it has visited. What does that cost?
Imagine two runners on a track, one twice as fast as the other. If the track is a loop, what must eventually happen?
Move `slow` 1 step and `fast` 2 steps per round. If `fast` reaches null there is no cycle; if they ever point to the same node there is one.

approaches.name: Hash set of visited nodes
approaches.idea: Store each node reference in a set; seeing a node twice means a cycle. Simple, but uses memory proportional to the list.

approaches.name: Mark nodes (destructive)
approaches.idea: Overwrite values or next pointers to mark visits. O(1) space but corrupts the input — usually not acceptable.

approaches.name: Floyd’s fast & slow pointers
approaches.idea: `fast` moves 2, `slow` moves 1. In a loop the gap shrinks by 1 per round, so they must meet.

solution.summary: Use Floyd’s tortoise and hare: move `slow` one node and `fast` two nodes per step. If `fast` hits null the list ends, so no cycle; if the two pointers ever reference the same node, there is a cycle. O(n) time, O(1) space.

code.code:
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next       # 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next  # 2 steps
        if slow is fast:       # same node object, not just same value
            return True
    return False

complexity.time: O(n) — slow is caught within one lap after entering the loop

keyPoints: Mention the hash-set solution first, then improve to O(1) space
Check `fast && fast.next` before jumping two steps
Compare node identity (`===`, `is`, `==` on references), never values
Explain why they meet: the gap shrinks by exactly one per round
Know the follow-up: reset one pointer to head to find the cycle start

Comparing `slow.val === fast.val` — different nodes can hold equal values
Checking `slow === fast` before moving — they start equal, so you would always return true
Using the visited-set approach without mentioning its O(n) memory cost

followUps.question: How do you find the node where the cycle begins?
followUps.answer: After slow and fast meet, move one pointer to head and advance both one step at a time; they meet at the cycle start because a = kL − b.

followUps.question: How do you compute the length of the cycle?
followUps.answer: From the meeting point, keep one pointer fixed and walk the other until it returns, counting steps.

followUps.question: Where else is Floyd’s algorithm used?
followUps.answer: "Find the duplicate number" in an array of n + 1 values in 1..n (treat i → nums[i] as a linked list), and detecting cycles in iterated functions such as the "happy number" problem.

questions.title: Middle of the Linked List
questions.prompt:
Given the `head` of a non-empty singly linked list, return the **middle node**. If the list has an even number of nodes there are two middle nodes — return the **second** one.

Try to do it in a single pass without counting the nodes first.

examples.explanation: Middles are 3 and 4; return the second.

hints: The obvious way counts the nodes first. Can you find the middle while walking only once?
If one pointer moves twice as fast as another, where is the slow one when the fast one finishes?
Loop while `fast && fast.next`: `slow` += 1, `fast` += 2. Return `slow`.

approaches.name: Copy into an array
approaches.idea: Push every node into an array and return `arr[Math.floor(n / 2)]`.

approaches.name: Two passes
approaches.idea: Count the nodes (n), then walk n / 2 steps from the head.

approaches.name: Fast & slow pointers
approaches.idea: One pass: fast moves 2, slow moves 1; when fast finishes, slow is at the middle.

solution.summary: Move a `slow` pointer one node and a `fast` pointer two nodes at a time; when `fast` can no longer move two steps, `slow` is at the middle. With the `fast && fast.next` condition, even-length lists return the second middle. One pass, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** After k rounds `slow` is at index k and `fast` is at index 2k. When `fast` reaches the end (index ≈ n − 1 or n), `slow` is at ≈ n / 2.

**Steps**
1. `slow = fast = head`.
2. While `fast` and `fast.next` are both non-null: `slow = slow.next`, `fast = fast.next.next`.
3. Return `slow`.

**Odd vs even.** For 5 nodes `fast` stops **on** the last node (fast.next is null) and `slow` is node 3. For 6 nodes `fast` steps **past** the last node (becomes null) and `slow` is node 4, the second middle.

**Need the first middle instead?** (e.g. to split a list in half for merge sort or reorder list) loop while `fast.next && fast.next.next`. Then for 6 nodes `slow` stops at node 3, the end of the first half.

complexity.time: O(n) — fast walks the list once

keyPoints: One pass with fast (2 steps) and slow (1 step)
`fast && fast.next` → second middle on even length
`fast.next && fast.next.next` → first middle (useful to split a list)
Same pattern powers cycle detection, palindrome check and reorder list

followUps.question: How would you delete the middle node?
followUps.answer: You need the node before it. Either keep a `prev` pointer that trails `slow` and finish with `prev.next = slow.next`, or start `fast` two steps ahead (`fast = head.next.next`) so that `slow` stops on the node just before the middle and you can set `slow.next = slow.next.next`. A single-node list simply becomes empty.

followUps.question: Why use this instead of counting?
followUps.answer: Both are O(n) time and O(1) space, but fast/slow needs one pass and the same pattern solves cycle detection and splitting — interviewers want to see it.

questions.title: Remove the N-th Node From the End
questions.prompt:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list and an integer `n`, delete the **n-th node counted from the end** (n = 1 is the last node) and return the head of the resulting list.

You are guaranteed that `1 ≤ n ≤ length`. Can you do it in one pass?

examples.explanation: Removing the head — the dummy node makes this case work without special code.

hints: n-th from the end is the (L − n + 1)-th from the start if you know the length L. Can you avoid computing L?
Two pointers that are always n nodes apart: when the front one reaches the end, where is the back one?
Start both at a dummy node, move `fast` n steps, then move both until `fast.next` is null; `slow.next` is the node to delete.

approaches.name: Two passes (count first)
approaches.idea: Count the length L, then walk L − n steps from a dummy node and unlink the next node.

approaches.name: Array of nodes

approaches.name: One pass, gap of n
approaches.idea: Advance `fast` n nodes ahead of `slow`, then move both until `fast` is on the last node.

solution.summary: Put a dummy node before the head, move `fast` n steps ahead, then move `fast` and `slow` together until `fast` is on the last node. `slow` is now just before the target, so `slow.next = slow.next.next`. One pass, O(1) space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** If two pointers stay exactly n nodes apart, the moment the front pointer is on the last node, the back pointer is n nodes before it — that is, right **before** the n-th node from the end.

**Steps**
1. `dummy = new ListNode(0, head)`; `fast = slow = dummy`.
2. Move `fast` forward n times.
3. While `fast.next` is not null, move both one step.
4. `slow.next = slow.next.next` unlinks the target.
5. Return `dummy.next` (not `head` — the head may have been removed).

**Why the dummy node?** To delete a node you need its predecessor. The head has no predecessor, so without a dummy you would need an `if` for "n equals the length". With the dummy, `slow` simply stays on it.

**Edge cases.** Single node with n = 1 → returns null. n = length → removes the head. n = 1 → removes the tail.

code.code:
def remove_nth_from_end(head, n):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)  # lets us remove the head too
    fast = slow = dummy
    for _ in range(n):  # open a gap of n nodes
        fast = fast.next
    while fast.next:  # until fast sits on the last node
        fast = fast.next
        slow = slow.next
    slow.next = slow.next.next  # slow is right before the target
    return dummy.next

complexity.time: O(L) — one pass over the list
complexity.space: O(1) — a dummy node and two pointers

questions.title: Reorder List (L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 …)
questions.prompt:
You are given the `head` of a singly linked list `L0 → L1 → … → Ln-1 → Ln`. Rearrange it **in place** into `L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → L2 → Ln-2 → …`.

Change the links, not the values stored in the nodes. The function returns nothing.
constraints: Only re-link nodes; do not swap values
hints: You keep needing "the last node not used yet". Which part of the list do you need to walk backwards?
If the second half were reversed, the nodes you need would come in the right order from two simple forward lists.
Three steps you already know: find the middle (fast/slow), reverse the second half, then merge the two halves alternately.

approaches.name: Repeatedly find the tail
approaches.idea: For each node in the first half, walk to the current tail, unlink it and insert it after that node.

approaches.name: Array of nodes + two pointers
approaches.idea: Store nodes in an array, then link nodes[0], nodes[n-1], nodes[1], nodes[n-2], …

approaches.name: Middle + reverse + weave
approaches.idea: Split at the middle with fast/slow, reverse the second half in place, interleave the two halves.

solution.summary: Combine three standard moves: find the middle with fast/slow pointers, cut and reverse the second half, then weave the first half and the reversed second half node by node. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** The pattern alternates "next from the front" and "next from the back". A singly linked list cannot walk backwards — unless we reverse the back half first. Then both halves can be read forwards.

**Steps**
1. **Middle.** `slow`/`fast` from head while `fast.next && fast.next.next`. `slow` stops at the end of the first half (for 5 nodes: node 3; for 4 nodes: node 2).
2. **Cut and reverse.** `curr = slow.next`, `slow.next = null`, then reverse from `curr` with the standard prev/curr/next loop. `prev` is the head of the reversed second half.
3. **Weave.** With `first = head` and `second = prev`: save both nexts, link `first → second → (old first.next)`, advance both. Stop when `second` is null — the first half is equal or one longer, so its last node is already in place.

**Why cut?** Without `slow.next = null` the last node of the first half would still point into the reversed half and the weave would create a cycle.

**Edge cases.** 1 or 2 nodes: nothing changes (early return handles one node; for two nodes the second half is a single node and the weave is a no-op).

code.code:
def reorder_list(head):
    if not head or not head.next:
        return
    # 1) find the end of the first half
    slow = fast = head
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    # 2) cut after slow and reverse the second half
    prev, curr = None, slow.next
    slow.next = None
    while curr:
        curr.next, prev, curr = prev, curr, curr.next
    # 3) weave: first, last, second, second-last, ...
    first, second = head, prev
    while second:
        n1, n2 = first.next, second.next
        first.next = second
        second.next = n1
        first, second = n1, n2

complexity.time: O(n) — three linear passes (middle, reverse, weave)

questions.title: Add Two Numbers Stored as Linked Lists
questions.prompt:
Two non-negative integers are stored as linked lists with **one digit per node, ones digit first** (so `2 → 4 → 3` is 342). Return their sum as a linked list in the same format.

The numbers have no leading zeros except the number 0 itself, and they may have different lengths — far more digits than fit in a 64-bit integer.

examples.explanation: 98 + 5 = 103: different lengths and a final carry

hints: The ones digit comes first — that is exactly the order in which you add numbers by hand.
Converting to a number overflows for 100 digits. Add digit by digit and keep a carry.
Loop while `l1 || l2 || carry`; treat a missing digit as 0; append `sum % 10`; carry = `Math.floor(sum / 10)`.

approaches.name: Convert to numbers
approaches.idea: Turn both lists into integers, add, convert back. Overflows 64-bit integers for long inputs (BigInt works in JS but misses the point).

approaches.name: Digit-by-digit with carry
approaches.idea: Walk both lists together, add digits plus carry, append one node per digit using a dummy head.
approaches.space: O(max(m, n)) for the output, O(1) extra

solution.summary: Simulate grade-school addition: walk both lists together, add the two digits plus the carry, append `sum % 10` to a new list built from a dummy node, and keep `sum / 10` as the carry. Continue while either list or the carry remains. O(max(m, n)) time.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** Because the ones digit is first, the lists are already in the order we add columns by hand — no reversal needed.

**Steps**
1. `dummy` node, `tail = dummy`, `carry = 0`.
2. While `l1` or `l2` or `carry` is non-zero:
   - `sum = carry + (l1?.val ?? 0) + (l2?.val ?? 0)`, advancing whichever lists are not finished.
   - Append a node with `sum % 10`; `carry = Math.floor(sum / 10)` (always 0 or 1).
3. Return `dummy.next`.

**Why `|| carry` in the loop condition?** 5 + 5 = 10 needs an extra node for the final carry; without it you would return just `0`.

**Edge cases.** Different lengths (the shorter one contributes 0), final carry (98 + 5 = 103), both numbers 0.

**Follow-up: digits stored most-significant first?** Either reverse both lists, add, and reverse the result, or push digits onto two stacks and pop them so you can add from the ones digit while building the answer from the front.

code.code:
def add_two_numbers(l1, l2):
    dummy = tail = ListNode(0)
    carry = 0
    while l1 or l2 or carry:
        total = carry
        if l1:
            total += l1.val
            l1 = l1.next
        if l2:
            total += l2.val
            l2 = l2.next
        carry, digit = divmod(total, 10)
        tail.next = ListNode(digit)  # one digit per node
        tail = tail.next
    return dummy.next

complexity.time: O(max(m, n)) — one step per digit of the longer number (+1 for a final carry)
complexity.space: O(max(m, n)) for the result list; O(1) besides the output

Do not convert to integers — overflow
Missing digits count as 0 so lists of different length work

questions.title: Palindrome Linked List
questions.prompt:
Given the `head` of a singly linked list, return `true` if the sequence of values reads the same forwards and backwards.

The easy version uses O(n) extra space; the follow-up asks for **O(n) time and O(1) extra space**.
hints: With an array you would compare `a[i]` with `a[n − 1 − i]`. What stops you from doing that on a list?
You need to read the second half backwards. Could you make it readable forwards instead?
Find the middle with fast/slow pointers, reverse from the middle, then walk one pointer from the head and one from the reversed half, comparing values.

approaches.idea: Copy values to an array and compare from both ends.

approaches.name: Stack of the first half
approaches.idea: Push the first half (found with fast/slow) on a stack, pop while walking the second half.

approaches.name: Reverse the second half
approaches.idea: Find the middle, reverse the second half in place, compare it with the first half.

solution.summary: Find the middle with fast/slow pointers, reverse the second half in place, then compare the first half and the reversed second half node by node. Any mismatch means false. O(n) time, O(1) extra space — and you can reverse the half back to restore the input.
solution.explanation:
**Intuition.** A palindrome compares position i with position n − 1 − i. In a singly linked list we can only walk forwards, so we reverse the **second half** — then both halves can be walked forwards in lockstep.

**Steps**
1. `slow`/`fast` while `fast && fast.next`: `slow` stops at the middle (odd length) or at the start of the second half (even length).
2. Reverse the list starting at `slow`; `prev` is the head of the reversed half.
3. Walk `left` from `head` and `right` from `prev` until `right` is null; any `left.val !== right.val` → false.
4. Return true.

**Why it works for both lengths.** Odd (1 2 3 2 1): the second half is 3 2 1 → reversed 1 2 3; both pointers meet on the shared middle node, which trivially equals itself. Even (1 2 2 1): second half 2 1 → reversed 1 2; the first half 1 → 2 still ends at the old middle, and `right` ends first.

**Being a good citizen.** This modifies the input. In production (or if asked) reverse the second half again before returning so the caller’s list is intact.

complexity.space: O(1) — in place (the array/stack versions are O(n))

questions.title: Design an LRU Cache
questions.prompt:
Design a **Least Recently Used (LRU) cache** with a fixed `capacity`:

- `get(key)` returns the value for `key`, or `-1` if it is not present. A successful `get` counts as using the key.
- `put(key, value)` inserts or updates the key. If inserting a new key would exceed `capacity`, first evict the **least recently used** key.

Both operations must run in **O(1) average time**. Implement it as a class.

examples.explanation: put(3,30) evicts key 2 (key 1 was used more recently); put(4,40) evicts key 1.
Updating an existing key does not evict anything.

constraints: Up to 2 · 10⁵ calls to get and put
get and put must be O(1) on average
hints: Which data structure gives O(1) lookup by key? Which one keeps an order where you can move an item to the front and drop the last item in O(1)?
A singly linked list cannot remove a node in O(1) unless you know its predecessor.
Hash map key → node of a doubly linked list ordered by recency. Use head/tail sentinels: `get` moves the node to the front, `put` inserts at the front and evicts `tail.prev` when full.

approaches.name: Array/list of (key, time)
approaches.idea: Scan to find a key or the oldest timestamp on every operation.

approaches.name: Hash map + ordered structure (TreeMap/heap by timestamp)
approaches.idea: Map key → timestamp plus a sorted structure to find the oldest.

approaches.name: Hash map + doubly linked list
approaches.idea: Map gives O(1) lookup of the node; the list keeps recency order with O(1) unlink/insert at the ends.

solution.summary: Combine a hash map from key to node with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. `get` looks the node up in the map and moves it to the front; `put` updates or inserts at the front and, when full, evicts the node just before the tail sentinel. Every step is O(1).
solution.explanation:
**Why two structures?**
- A **hash map** answers "where is key k?" in O(1) — but it has no notion of order.
- A **doubly linked list** keeps the order of use: most recent at the front, least recent at the back. With a pointer to a node, unlinking it is O(1) because the node knows its `prev`. A singly linked list would need an O(n) search for the predecessor.

**Sentinels.** Dummy `head` and `tail` nodes mean the list is never empty, so `remove` and `addFront` have no null checks.

**Operations**
- `get(key)`: look up the node; if missing return -1. Otherwise `remove(node)`, `addFront(node)`, return its value.
- `put(key, value)`: if the key exists, unlink its old node. Else if the cache is full, take `lru = tail.prev`, unlink it and **delete `lru.key` from the map** (this is why each node stores its key). Then create a node, put it in the map and `addFront` it.

**Language shortcuts (say them, but be ready to implement the real thing)**
- Java: `LinkedHashMap` with `accessOrder = true` and an overridden `removeEldestEntry`.
- Python: `collections.OrderedDict` with `move_to_end` and `popitem(last=False)`.
- JavaScript: a `Map` iterates in insertion order — delete and re-set a key to mark it recent; `map.keys().next().value` is the LRU key.

**Real systems.** Page caches in operating systems, database buffer pools, CDN and browser caches and Redis' `allkeys-lru` eviction policy all use LRU or approximations of it.

complexity.time: O(1) average for get and put — one hash lookup plus a constant number of pointer changes
complexity.space: O(capacity) — one map entry and one list node per key

keyPoints: Hash map for O(1) lookup, doubly linked list for O(1) reordering and eviction
Doubly linked because removing a node needs its predecessor
Sentinel head/tail remove all null edge cases
Store the key inside the node so eviction can delete it from the map
A successful get also updates recency
Know the built-ins: LinkedHashMap, OrderedDict, JS Map insertion order

followUps.question: How would you make it thread-safe?
followUps.answer: The simplest correct answer is one lock around get and put (both mutate the list). For high concurrency, shard the cache into N independent LRU segments by key hash, each with its own lock, or use an approximate policy (e.g. Caffeine’s W-TinyLFU in Java).

followUps.question: What about LFU (least frequently used)?
followUps.answer: Keep key → (value, freq) and freq → doubly linked list of keys, plus the current minimum frequency. get/put move a key from list f to list f + 1; eviction removes the LRU key of the min-frequency list. Still O(1).

followUps.question: How would you add expiry (TTL)?
followUps.answer: Store an expiry timestamp in each node; treat expired nodes as misses on get (lazy deletion) and optionally run a periodic sweep or a min-heap by expiry time.

questions.title: Array vs Linked List — when would you use each?
questions.prompt: Compare **arrays** (including dynamic arrays such as `ArrayList`, Python `list`, JS arrays) with **linked lists**. Cover memory layout, the cost of common operations, and when you would choose each in a real program.
hints: Start from memory: how are the elements laid out, and how do you find the i-th one?
Go operation by operation: access by index, insert/delete at the front, middle and end, search.
Do not forget the CPU cache — Big-O alone does not decide which is faster in practice.

approaches.name: Weak answer
approaches.idea: "Arrays are fixed size, linked lists are dynamic; linked lists are faster for insertion." Partly outdated (dynamic arrays grow) and missing the conditions (you need the node first) and the cache argument.

approaches.name: Strong answer
approaches.idea: Explains contiguous vs node-based memory, gives the complexity table with conditions (O(1) insert only given the node), amortised O(1) append, cache locality and per-node overhead, and names real uses (LRU cache, deques, OS free lists) vs the default choice of dynamic arrays.

solution.summary: An array stores elements contiguously, so index access is O(1) and it is very cache-friendly, but inserting or deleting in the middle shifts elements (O(n)). A linked list stores separate nodes joined by pointers, so inserting or removing next to a node you already hold is O(1), but reaching the i-th element is O(n) and every node costs extra pointer memory. Default to a dynamic array; use a linked list when you splice at known positions, like an LRU cache.
solution.explanation:
**Memory layout**
- **Array:** one contiguous block. The address of `a[i]` is `base + i × elementSize`, so access is one multiplication — O(1). A **dynamic array** (Java `ArrayList`, Python `list`, C++ `vector`, JS arrays) over-allocates and, when full, copies everything into a bigger block (typically 1.5× – 2×), which makes `append` **amortised O(1)**.
- **Linked list:** each node is a separate allocation holding the value plus a `next` pointer (and `prev` in a doubly linked list). Nodes can be anywhere in memory, so to reach the i-th node you must follow i pointers.

**Operation costs**
| Operation | Dynamic array | Singly linked list | Doubly linked list |
|---|---|---|---|
| Access i-th | O(1) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Search by value | O(n) (O(log n) if sorted, via binary search) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Insert/delete at front | O(n) (shift) | O(1) | O(1) |
| Append at end | amortised O(1) | O(1) with a tail pointer | O(1) |
| Insert/delete in the middle | O(n) shift | O(1) **after** you have the previous node; finding it is O(n) | O(1) given the node itself |

**What Big-O hides**
- **Cache locality:** iterating an array streams through memory the CPU prefetches; a linked list jumps between random addresses and causes cache misses. In practice an array often wins even for workloads with some middle insertions.
- **Memory overhead:** each node carries one or two pointers (8 bytes each on a 64-bit machine) plus allocator/object-header overhead — for small values the list can use several times more memory.
- Binary search, sorting with random access, and SIMD-friendly loops all need arrays.

**When to use a linked list**
- You already hold references to nodes and need O(1) removal/re-insertion: **LRU cache** (hash map + doubly linked list), OS process/free lists, intrusive lists in kernels.
- Queues/deques where both ends change and you cannot afford an occasional O(n) resize (though ring buffers like Java's `ArrayDeque` are usually better).
- Splicing/concatenating whole lists in O(1).

**When to use an array (most of the time)**
Random access, iteration-heavy code, binary search, memory-sensitive data, anything sorted. In Java, prefer `ArrayList`/`ArrayDeque` over `LinkedList` unless you have a measured reason.

Real linked-list uses: LRU cache, deques, OS free lists; default to arrays otherwise

followUps.question: Why is ArrayList append amortised O(1) if resizing copies everything?
followUps.answer: Capacity grows geometrically (≈1.5× in Java’s ArrayList), so a copy of size n happens only after about n/2 cheap appends; the total copy work over n appends is O(n), i.e. O(1) per append on average.

followUps.question: When would you choose a doubly over a singly linked list?
followUps.answer: When you must delete a node given only a reference to it, or traverse backwards (LRU cache, browser history, deques). The cost is one extra pointer per node and more pointer updates per operation.

followUps.question: How is a queue implemented efficiently?
followUps.answer: Either a linked list with head and tail pointers (O(1) enqueue/dequeue) or, usually better, a circular array buffer (Java ArrayDeque) that avoids per-node allocation.

quiz.question: Given only the head, what is the time complexity of reaching the k-th node of a singly linked list?
options: O(log k)
O(k)
O(k log k)
quiz.explanation: There is no index arithmetic: you must follow k `next` pointers one by one. O(1) access is the array’s advantage, because its elements are contiguous.

quiz.question: Why do many linked-list solutions create a dummy node in front of the head?
options: It turns the list into a doubly linked list
Operations that change or remove the head then need no special case
It makes traversal O(log n)
Garbage collectors require it to free nodes
quiz.explanation: With a dummy, every real node — including the head — has a predecessor, so "insert before" and "delete" work uniformly. You return `dummy.next` at the end.

quiz.question: What does this print?
options: 1 null
3 { val: 2, next: { val: 1, next: null } }
1 { val: 2, next: { val: 3, next: null } }
TypeError: Cannot read properties of null
quiz.explanation: The reversal works, but its return value (the new head, node 3) is ignored. `head` still references node 1, which is now the tail, so `head.next` is `null`. Always use the returned head.

quiz.question: In Floyd’s cycle detection, why can the fast pointer (2 steps) never jump over the slow pointer (1 step) inside the loop?
options: Because loop lengths are always even
Because fast checks every node it passes over
It can — that is why a third pointer is sometimes needed
Because the forward distance from fast to slow shrinks by exactly one node per round
quiz.explanation: Each round fast gains 2 and slow gains 1, so the gap decreases by exactly 1 and must reach 0 — they land on the same node. No third pointer is needed.

quiz.question: After slow and fast meet inside a cycle, how do you find the first node of the cycle?
options: The meeting node is always the first node of the cycle
Count the loop length and walk half of it from the head
Move one pointer back to head, then advance both one step at a time until they meet
Reverse the list and run Floyd’s algorithm again
quiz.explanation: If a = head→start and b = start→meeting point, then 2(a + b) = a + b + kL gives a = kL − b. Walking a steps from the head and from the meeting point ends at the cycle start.

quiz.question: Both pointers start at the head of 1 → 2 → 3 → 4. After `while (fast && fast.next) { slow = slow.next; fast = fast.next.next; }`, where is slow?
options: Node 3
Node 2
Node 4
null
quiz.explanation: Round 1: slow = 2, fast = 3. Round 2: slow = 3, fast = null (stepped past node 4). The loop stops with slow on node 3, the second of the two middles.

quiz.question: How much extra space does the recursive reversal of an n-node list use?
options: O(log n)
O(n²)
O(n) for the call stack
quiz.explanation: Each node adds one stack frame before the base case is reached, so the stack grows to n frames. That is why the iterative three-pointer version (O(1) space) is preferred, and why very long lists can overflow the stack.

quiz.question: Why does an LRU cache use a doubly linked list rather than a singly linked list?
options: A doubly linked list uses less memory
Unlinking an arbitrary node in O(1) needs its predecessor, which only a doubly linked node stores
Hash maps can only point to doubly linked nodes
It allows binary search over the keys
quiz.explanation: The map hands you the node; to remove it you must update `node.prev.next`. In a singly linked list finding the predecessor costs O(n). The trade-off is one extra pointer per node.

quiz.question: In the hash map + doubly linked list LRU cache, why does each list node also store its key?
options: To keep the list sorted by key
To make hashing faster
So that when the tail node is evicted, its entry can also be deleted from the hash map
Doubly linked lists cannot work without keys
quiz.explanation: Eviction starts from the list (`tail.prev`), not from the map. Without the key inside the node you would not know which map entry to delete, and the map would keep a stale reference.

quiz.question: Add Two Numbers (digits stored ones-first): l1 = 5 and l2 = 5, each a single node. What must be returned?
quiz.explanation: 5 + 5 = 10: digit 0 with carry 1, then one more node for the carry. Ones digit first gives 0 → 1. Returning just 0 is the classic bug of not looping while `carry !== 0`.

quiz.question: Which operation is clearly faster on a dynamic array than on a linked list?
options: Inserting at the front
Removing a node you already hold a reference to (doubly linked)
Splicing two lists together
Reading the element at index i
quiz.explanation: Index access is O(1) on an array (base + i × size) but O(i) on a list. The other three are O(1) on a linked list and O(n) (or worse) on an array.

quiz.question: Removing the n-th node from the end: both pointers start at a dummy node, fast moves n steps, then both move while `fast.next !== null`. Where does slow stop?
options: On the node to remove
On the node just before the node to remove
On the last node
Always on the dummy node
quiz.explanation: When fast is on the last node, slow is n nodes behind it — the predecessor of the n-th node from the end — which is exactly what `slow.next = slow.next.next` needs.
